sections.content: San Diego is one of the most competitive real estate markets in the country — and for good reason. Strong job growth, year-round sunshine, a massive military presence, and a steady flow of tourists and transplants keep demand consistently high. But high demand also means higher prices, which makes finding truly profitable real estate deals in San Diego CA a skill that separates successful investors from the rest. Whether you're a local wholesaler, a flipper looking for your next project, or an out-of-state investor eyeing this coastal market, this guide will give you a clear, honest look at what the San Diego market offers in 2024. If you're brand new to investing, start with our Real Estate Investing for Beginners guide before diving into a market this competitive.
San Diego Market Overview: What Investors Need to Know

San Diego County has a population of over 3.3 million people and one of the lowest housing vacancy rates in California. The city consistently ranks among the top 10 most expensive housing markets in the United States. As of mid-2024, the median home price in San Diego sits at approximately $900,000 to $950,000 — a number that can intimidate investors used to Midwest or Sun Belt pricing. However, that headline number doesn't tell the whole story. Pockets of the market offer entry points well below that median, especially in emerging neighborhoods and distressed property segments. The key is knowing where to look and how to run the numbers correctly.
In expensive markets like San Diego, the deal is everything. You can't rely on the market to bail you out — you have to buy right from day one.
Best Neighborhoods for Real Estate Investors in San Diego

San Diego is not a monolithic market. The county spans 18 incorporated cities and dozens of distinct neighborhoods, each with its own price point, tenant profile, and investment potential. Targeting the right zip code can mean the difference between a home run deal and a money pit. Here are the neighborhoods and submarkets that investors are watching closely in 2024.
Value-Add and Wholesale Opportunities

items: City Heights: One of San Diego's most diverse neighborhoods with median prices around $600,000–$700,000. High renter population, strong cash flow potential, and older housing stock that creates fix-and-flip opportunities.

Southeast San Diego (Encanto, Lincoln Park): Entry-level pricing for San Diego with medians in the $550,000–$650,000 range. Gentrification pressure is creating equity-building opportunities for early movers.
Chula Vista: Rapidly growing suburb just south of downtown with new development and strong rental demand. Prices range from $650,000–$800,000 depending on the area.
El Cajon and Santee: East County markets with more affordable price points ($550,000–$700,000) and strong blue-collar rental demand. Good for buy-and-hold investors.
National City: Densely populated with high renter-to-owner ratios. Smaller multi-family properties can still be found at prices that pencil out for cash flow.

sections.content: Premium Flip and BRRRR Markets

items: North Park and South Park: Trendy urban neighborhoods where renovated homes regularly sell for $900,000–$1.2M. Strong ARVs reward quality flips.
Lemon Grove and Spring Valley: Transitional suburbs with distressed inventory and buyers willing to pay updated-home premiums.
Oceanside: Coastal access at more accessible price points than La Jolla or Del Mar. Strong vacation rental and long-term rental demand near Camp Pendleton.

sections.content: Types of Real Estate Deals Available in San Diego
Wholesale Deals

Wholesaling in San Diego is possible but requires hustle. Assignment fees in this market can run $20,000 to $60,000 or more on a single deal because of the high underlying values — but finding sellers willing to accept a significant discount takes consistent lead generation. Motivated sellers here often include estate sales, pre-foreclosures (California's non-judicial foreclosure process moves fast), tired landlords dealing with California's strict tenant protection laws, and inherited properties. If you want to learn the mechanics of the strategy first, check out our guide on Wholesaling Real Estate for Beginners. For deal sourcing strategies, our article on How to Find Off-Market Real Estate Deals is essential reading before you start dialing for dollars in San Diego.
Fix and Flip

Fix-and-flip investing is alive and well in San Diego, but margins are tight if you overpay. A typical flip in a neighborhood like North Park or City Heights might involve purchasing a dated 3-bed/1-bath home for $650,000, investing $80,000–$120,000 in renovation, and selling for $900,000–$950,000. That leaves a gross profit of $130,000–$200,000 before carrying costs, commissions, and taxes. Always run a detailed ARV analysis before committing. Use our free ARV Calculator to estimate your after-repair value based on comparable sales in the specific submarket you're targeting.
Rental Properties and the BRRRR Strategy

San Diego's rents are among the highest in California, with average 2-bedroom rents hovering around $2,800–$3,200 per month depending on location. This makes long-term rental investing appealing, though traditional cash flow is challenging at current price points without a meaningful down payment or value-add angle. The BRRRR method (Buy, Rehab, Rent, Refinance, Repeat) works well here when you can acquire a distressed property at 70–75 cents on the dollar, force equity through renovation, and refinance to pull capital back out for your next deal. Small multi-family properties (duplexes and triplexes) in City Heights, National City, and Chula Vista are especially worth pursuing.

Pro Tip: California's AB 1482 rent control law caps annual rent increases at 5% + local CPI (max 10%) on properties older than 15 years. Factor this into your long-term cash flow projections before buying a rental in San Diego — and always verify whether the specific property qualifies for an exemption.
San Diego Real Estate Market Trends in 2024

items: Inventory remains historically low, keeping upward pressure on prices despite elevated mortgage rates.
Days on market have increased slightly from 2022 highs, giving buyers slightly more negotiating room — but still averaging just 20–30 days for desirable properties.
Short-term rental demand remains strong near the coast, though San Diego has tightened its STR regulations. Check current licensing requirements before buying for Airbnb use.
New construction is concentrated in East County and South County suburbs, with very little new supply in infill urban neighborhoods — supporting appreciation in older housing stock.

Military relocation demand from Marine Corps Base Camp Pendleton, Naval Station San Diego, and Miramar creates consistent year-round rental demand that insulates the market from some economic downturns.

sections.content: Tips for Out-of-State Investors Targeting San Diego

San Diego attracts significant interest from investors in other states, particularly those looking to diversify into a stable coastal market. But investing remotely in a high-cost, highly regulated state like California requires more preparation than investing locally. Here's what out-of-state investors need to get right before deploying capital in this market.

items: Build your local team first: You need a reliable investor-friendly real estate agent, a contractor network, and a property manager before you close your first deal — not after.

Understand California landlord-tenant law: California is among the most tenant-protective states in the country. Evictions can take 3–6 months. Know the rules around security deposits, habitability standards, and just-cause eviction requirements.
Use data, not gut feelings: At these price points, every deal must be underwritten rigorously. Learn how to analyze real estate deals like a pro before making offers.
Visit the market at least once: San Diego's neighborhoods vary dramatically block-by-block. A virtual tour cannot replace walking the streets of City Heights versus Chula Vista versus Oceanside.

Watch your cost basis obsessively: California transfer taxes, high property taxes on purchase price, and mandatory disclosure requirements add to closing costs. Use our free Wholesale Deal Calculator to stress-test every offer before you submit it.

sections.content: The investors who lose money in expensive markets like San Diego aren't the ones who couldn't find deals — they're the ones who overpaid because they fell in love with the location instead of the numbers.

Pro Tip: Connect with the San Diego Creative Investors Association (SDCIA) — one of the most active REIA groups in Southern California. Monthly meetings attract local wholesalers, agents, and lenders who can help you build your team and find your first deal faster than going it alone.
Where to Find Deals in the San Diego Market Right Now

On-market MLS deals in San Diego rarely offer the margins investors need. The real money is in off-market properties: direct mail to pre-foreclosure lists, probate leads, absentee owners, and code violation properties. Driving for dollars in transitional neighborhoods like Southeast San Diego and El Cajon can surface distressed properties before they hit the market.
